content: In 2020, approximately 604,000 new cases of cervical cancer were reported globally. Screening is crucial as it helps detect precancerous lesions at stages where they can be treated effectively. As a result, cervical cancer is often diagnosed at more advanced stages, when symptoms have already developed. Additionally, access to treatment options such as cancer surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy is often restricted in LMICs, leading to higher mortality rates from cervical cancer in these regions. The vast majority of cervical cancer cases (over 95%) are caused by HPV, which is the most common viral infection of the reproductive tract. Most sexually active individuals, both men and women, will be infected with HPV at some point in their lives, and some may experience repeated infections. While more than 90% of infected individuals eventually clear the virus, chronic infections can lead to precancerous lesions and invasive cancer. Some countries have also started vaccinating boys, as the vaccine prevents HPV-related diseases and cancers in males. The HPV vaccine is a key component of adolescent health programs. Both girls and boys should receive age-appropriate health information, including sex education. Condoms should be promoted and made available to sexually active individuals. Male circumcision should be encouraged. HPV vaccines have been proven to be safe and effective in preventing HPV infections, high-grade precancerous lesions, and invasive cancers. Currently, six vaccines are licensed, and four are prequalified by WHO. All of these vaccines protect against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for at least 70% of cervical cancers. The nine-valent vaccine also protects against five additional oncogenic HPV types, which account for another 20% of cervical cancers. Two of the vaccines also protect against HPV types 6 and 11, which cause anogenital warts. As of December 2022, 125 countries (64%) have introduced the HPV vaccine into their national immunization programs for girls, and 47 countries (24%) have extended this to boys. To address vision loss in adolescents, WHO recommends: Increasing access to spectacles or contact lenses, which can fully correct vision problems caused by myopia and other refractive errors. Spectacles are among the most practical and cost-effective healthcare interventions. Regular screening for refractive errors in preschool and school-aged children to prevent academic challenges due to poor vision. Public health campaigns to reduce time spent on near-vision activities and encourage outdoor activities to slow the progression of myopia. To address hearing loss in adolescents, WHO recommends: Raising awareness among adolescents, parents, and teachers about healthy ear care and safe listening practices to prevent noise-induced hearing loss. Implementing WHO global standards for safe listening in entertainment venues to protect young people’s hearing at concerts and clubs. Conducting regular school-based screenings for ear and hearing problems to enable early identification and timely management. Mental health conditions among adolescents are alarmingly prevalent, with up to 50% of all mental health conditions beginning before the age of 14. Approximately one in five adolescents experiences a mental disorder each year, and suicide is a leading cause of death among older adolescents. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated these issues, increasing the risk of suicide, substance use, and other mental health problems, particularly among adolescents in challenging situations such as prolonged conflicts. WHO emphasizes the importance of policies and laws to address the socioeconomic determinants of adolescent mental health, strengthen care systems, guide training programs for frontline workers, and inform public health monitoring and research. Community-based mental health services, integrated into general healthcare and non-health settings like schools, are essential. These services should include: Training school staff in whole-school approaches to mental health, including suicide prevention and crisis management. Establishing committees to plan and evaluate mental health initiatives involving educators, students, parents, and community leaders. Developing school policies on anti-bullying, respectful relationships, and child protection. Implementing school-based programs to enhance cognitive, problem-solving, and social skills. Supporting community interventions to reduce child abuse, neglect, and bullying. To prevent adolescent suicide, WHO recommends: Adopting national mental health policies focused on leadership, governance, prevention strategies, and evidence-based research. Restricting access to means of suicide, such as pesticides, firearms, and medications, and implementing infrastructure interventions to prevent suicide by jumping. Promoting responsible media reporting to avoid sensationalism and educate the public about suicide prevention. Improving access to mental health and substance use disorder treatments to reduce suicidal behavior. Developing long-term surveillance systems to monitor suicide cases and self-harm incidents for prevention and intervention. To address substance use among adolescents, WHO highlights the importance of: Strengthening restrictions on alcohol and drug availability through laws and policies, including reducing alcohol outlet density and setting minimum age limits for alcohol purchase and consumption. Banning or restricting alcohol advertising, sponsorship, and promotion, including in digital media. Raising alcohol prices through excise taxes and pricing policies to reduce harmful use and generate government revenue. Providing access to screening, brief interventions, and treatment for substance use disorders. Family-based and parenting programs play a critical role in preventing substance use. A warm parenting style that sets clear rules, monitors adolescents’ activities, and fosters personal and social skills is a powerful protective factor against risky behaviors. Finally, addressing tobacco use among adolescents is crucial, as tobacco kills up to half of its users and exposes others to second-hand smoke. Nicotine in tobacco products and electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS), such as e-cigarettes, is highly addictive and harmful to adolescent brain development.
